1:
The argument says people are happy with their banks because they don't change them, using the 11% who never switched. A shows the opposite: almost two-thirds have changed, some many times, so not changing is not the typical behaviour and the evidence collapses.
C would strengthen; B, D and E don't show that the 11% figure misrepresents customers.
5:
The argument jumps from "there is a conflict between the right to know and the patient's health" to "doctors must deceive". That only follows if health/well-being matters more than the right to the truth — that is D.
B is stronger than the argument (it says deceiving is needed only when health would worsen, not whenever the truth is frightening); C and E point the other way; A is about patients' views, which the argument never uses.
13: The argument treats road traffic work as just "obtaining money from road users", separate from protecting the public. But many traffic offences (e.g. dangerous or drunk driving) are crimes that endanger people, so traffic policing is protecting citizens — A.
2:
Conclusion: treating drug-dependent prisoners (heavy users) will reduce drug-related social problems. D supports exactly the link the argument needs: if heavy users commit most drug-related crime, treating them cuts the problem.
C weakens; A and B are about supply, which the argument has already set aside; E is about public opinion, not effectiveness.
3:
The passage gives a reason (two-year degrees lower graduate quality) and a principle (universities should resist anything that lowers quality). Together they give B: universities should oppose two-year degrees.
A goes beyond the passage; C, D and E are not supported.
4:
Premises: pesticides stay effective only if there are periods without use; GM plants produce pesticide continuously (no breaks). So their pesticide will stop working against pests — A.
D contradicts 'continuously'; B, C and E are not supported.
6:
The argument rules out genes and concludes diet causes Europe's higher cancer rates. C offers another difference between Europe and developing countries — stress — that could explain the pattern, so diet is no longer the only candidate.
A is about developing countries only; B, D and E don't offer a rival cause of the gap.
7:
The 'only fair solution' is a levy on top athletes, because otherwise the cost falls on taxpayers or families. Rejecting the taxpayer option only works if it is unfair for taxpayers to pay — C.
A, B, D and E are not needed for the reasoning.
8:
The argument says farmed fish is no answer because the wild fish fed to farmed fish would disappear. That assumes farming depends on wild fish as food — D.
A is too strong; B, C and E are not used.
9:
Everything in the passage (the stealing example, the tone/exclamation-mark comparison) supports the first sentence: adding 'right' or 'wrong' adds nothing to the factual content — A.
B is the example used as evidence; E explains what such words do instead; C contradicts the passage; D is not discussed.
10:
The passage says ecotourism is meant to be sustainable, then lists serious harms to wildlife (diseases, stress, lower breeding). So the benefits may be outweighed by harm — E.
A, C and D add claims the passage doesn't make; B goes against its drift.
11:
The passage rejects the 'naive view' about family planning and gives reasons why poor families want many children. The final 'It follows that…' sentence is the conclusion: only economic development can solve overpopulation — D.
B and E are steps along the way; A and C are not claimed.
12:
Conclusion: more rural pubs are needed or drink-driving will rise, because rural people must drive. D strengthens it: if the rural population grows, more people face this problem, so the risk of more drink-driving grows.
A, B and E don't affect the rural argument; C suggests rural pubs aren't wanted.
14:
The passage lists three funding options and gives a drawback for taxation (independence) and for commercial funding (advertisers' influence). The only option left without a drawback is the licence fee, so it is the best of imperfect options — C.
A is too strong ('no alternative'), B is too strong ('inevitably'), D and E are not discussed.
15:
The argument says people who don't want their brain chemistry altered should choose psychotherapy instead of drugs. That only works if psychotherapy itself doesn't alter brain chemistry — E.
A is not needed (the reason is preference, not effectiveness); B, C and D are not used.
16:
The reasons (signals don't impress, our ancestors were balanced) lead to: 'To be truly happy now, we should devote more time to the activities that dominated life back then' — D.
A and C are reasons; B is too vague; E is not stated.
17:
Add the rows over all ages (same number in each group): Drink B 20+31+33+19 = 103, no preference 33+12+22+34 = 101. So more people preferred B than had no preference — B.
A fails at 25–35 (32 vs 33); C fails (48 vs 52 for ages 5–15); D fails (225 of 400 had a preference); E fails (74 of 400 = 18.5%).
18:
The argument says stop using pesticides and let predator insects control the pests. It ignores that pesticides might control pests far better than those insects — A.
B and C point to gaps that would not undermine the argument as directly; D and E are irrelevant.
19:
The passage argues against removing small coins: prices would rise (consumers lose) and savers and charities lose the coins' value. So consumers and charities would lose out — E.
A and D are recommendations the passage doesn't make; B and C contradict it.
20:
The argument says cutting costs to push through more graduates would not serve students or long-term prosperity, and education has wider purposes. That depends on cost-cutting harming what universities are for — D.
A and B each pick one purpose; C is far too strong; E is not assumed.
21:
The plan works only if police can catch up after taking the turns. C supports that: police can keep faster speeds than other drivers, so following the likely route will close the gap.
B is about TV, not real chases; A, D and E are irrelevant or weaken.
22:
Spending per head of over-65s varies, and the argument concludes treatment depends on where you live. That only follows if the disease is equally common everywhere — otherwise low spending could just mean fewer patients. Assumption C.
D is already handled ('per head of the population over 65').
23:
Conclusion: stores shouldn't sell financial products because staff don't understand them and mislead customers. A gives evidence that mis-selling actually happens.
C and D weaken; B and E don't show misleading sales.
24:
The evidence is that the public and media turned against the President. The conclusion is that America is 'heaving with free debate'. This assumes that turning against the administration shows free debate is taking place — B.
A reverses the direction; C, D and E are not needed.
25:
The argument: ban child labour because work denies children their education. C undermines this: without the children's wages the family couldn't pay for school anyway, so a ban wouldn't give them an education.
A, B, D and E don't touch the education link.
26:
The passage praises the traditional system for precision and condemns today's careless comma use as lazy. The natural conclusion is to return to teaching the traditional system — C.
D goes too far (reopening grammar schools); A, B and E are not supported.
27:
The argument uses the average repair cost to say warranties are poor value for everyone. B shows the average hides that most products need no repairs while a few need costly ones — the warranty protects against those few big bills.
C actually supports the average; A, D and E don't weaken the value claim.
28:
Conclusion: private lives should be reported because they give insight into a leader's values. E strengthens it: politicians claim to be respectable in all parts of life, so reporting their private lives tests those claims.
A, B and D are irrelevant; C weakens.
29:
The argument credits the cameras with the fall in crime. C gives another cause: cameras usually come with extra police, so the fall may be due to the police.
A, B, D and E don't explain the drop another way.
30:
The argument says First Class makes Standard Class worse. B shows the opposite effect: First Class revenue benefits the whole service, including Standard Class.
A, C, D and E don't counter the claim that First Class harms other passengers.
